summary_html: Federal transparency statutes—**FOIA** and **Sunshine Act**—require disclosure of government data. Project Milk Carton promotes FOIA requests and public dashboards for child-welfare records.
authority_html:
- **Freedom of Information Act (5 U.S.C. § 552)** — public access to records  
- **Government in the Sunshine Act (5 U.S.C. § 552b)** — open-meeting requirements

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Allegheny County Department of Administrative Services v. A Second Chance, Inc.
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed in part and vacated in part, holding that the Right-to-Know Law's definition of 'record' is not confined to documents the agency itself created or holds, that agency policy bulletins could not create an exemption, and remanding for findings on the contractor's duties.
key_cases.relevance: The leading Pennsylvania RTKL decision on records held by a private child-welfare contractor for a county agency.
key_cases.quote: This language does not limit "record" to only those documents "created, received or retained" by the agency.

key_cases.case_name: In re Fortieth Statewide Investigating Grand Jury
key_cases.holding: The court ordered interim release of the clergy-abuse grand jury report with the challengers' identities redacted, holding that Pennsylvania's constitutional right to reputation requires enhanced procedural protections before a grand jury report publicly condemns named individuals.
key_cases.relevance: Establishes that redaction, not suppression, is the default remedy when reputation rights collide with public access.
key_cases.quote: the lines between a grand jury "investigation" and an "adjudication" are blurred when the grand jury renders wide-scale, individualized, condemnatory findings

key_cases.case_name: G.V. v. Department of Public Welfare
key_cases.holding: Reversing the Commonwealth Court, the court held that an indicated report of child abuse may be entered and maintained on the statewide ChildLine Registry on the CPSL's legislatively prescribed substantial-evidence standard, and that due process does not require clear and convincing evidence at an expunction hearing.
key_cases.relevance: The court's account of the CPSL's confidentiality and disclosure architecture governs transparency claims about registry data.
key_cases.quote: the proper standard of proof is the legislatively established substantial evidence standard

key_cases.case_name: Support Center for Child Advocates v. Department of Human Services
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of the child's guardian ad litem's petition to intervene in the alleged perpetrator's ChildLine expunction appeal, holding the GAL had no statutory right to intervene and no interest not already represented by the Department.
key_cases.relevance: Shows that even a child's court-appointed advocate has no general right of entry into confidential registry proceedings.
key_cases.quote: H.M.'s G.A.L. has no right to intervene "conferred by statute," nor has he stated an interest such that his participation "is in the public interest."

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: Affirming in part and reversing in part, the Court held that due process entitles a criminal defendant to have Pennsylvania's confidential CYS child-abuse file reviewed in camera by the trial court for material exculpatory evidence, but does not entitle defense counsel to search the file itself.
key_cases.relevance: Holds that a confidentiality scheme which itself contemplates court-ordered disclosure is not an absolute bar, so access disputes are resolved by judicial review rather than by agency refusal.
key_cases.quote: Although we recognize that the public interest in protecting this type of sensitive information is strong, we do not agree that this interest necessarily prevents disclosure in all circumstances.

key_cases.case_name: R. v. Department of Public Welfare
key_cases.holding: Affirming the Commonwealth Court, the court held that an alleged perpetrator was not denied due process at a ChildLine expunction hearing where the hearing examiner who decided the case had not observed all the witnesses and the child testified in camera subject to cross-examination, because the CPSL narrowly limits who may learn of an indicated report.
key_cases.relevance: Explains why the CPSL's restrictions on disclosure of an indicated report survive constitutional scrutiny, setting the baseline against which transparency claims are measured.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that R. received all the process he was due under the Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution
